# Introduction

Metaproteomes are usually compared by accession: Bray-Curtis, or a test per
protein, treats two different proteins as unrelated even when they share fold
and function. Proteins of one function in different organisms are often too
far apart in sequence for a sequence clustering to join them. `repdist`
compares proteins by their embeddings from a protein language model, by
default TM-Vec. The TM-score is a measure of structural similarity between
two proteins, from 0 to 1; above about 0.5 they usually share a fold. TM-Vec
is trained so that the cosine similarity of two embeddings is the predicted
TM-score, without needing a structure.

The embeddings serve two jobs that do not depend on each other:

- **protein bins**: `protein_similarity()` and `bin_proteins()` group
    structurally similar proteins by Markov clustering. This needs only the
    proteins and their embeddings, not a count table or any sample, so it
    works as a stand-alone protein clustering;
- **beta diversity**: `sample_mmd()` gives a sample-by-sample distance, the
    maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between the samples' abundance-weighted
    distributions over the embeddings. This needs no bins.

`bin_glom()` then sums a count table within bins, so that any differential
abundance method can test bins instead of single proteins. The goal is to see
a change in what the proteins do, not only in which accessions are present.

## The simulated data

`simulate_cog` is a simulated experiment, built from the NCBI COG 2024
release (Galperin et al. 2025) so that the answer is known. Twenty
metaproteome samples, ten in group A and ten in group B, share the same 100
background proteins, drawn at random from other COGs. What differs is one
function: each group-A sample also holds a GrpE protein, the nucleotide
exchange factor of the HSP-70 chaperone (COG0576), which no group-B sample
holds.

The design is meant to defeat a comparison by accession. Each group-A sample
holds a *different* GrpE protein, and the ten come from ten different
30%-identity MMseqs2 clusters, so no protein and no sequence family is
enriched in more than one sample. A test on accessions sees ten rare
proteins; only a method that recognises the ten as one function, GrpE, sees
the group-A enrichment. `?simulate_cog` gives the details, and
`inst/scripts/make_simulate_cog.R` how it was built.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Samples | 20: 10 in group A, 10 in group B |
| Background | 100 proteins from other COGs, in every sample |
| Treatment | 10 GrpE proteins (COG0576), one per group-A sample |
| Remote homology | each GrpE protein in its own MMseqs2 30%-identity cluster |
| Perturbation | 5% of each group-A sample's abundance on its GrpE protein (3.6-6.9% after sampling) |
| Counts | negative binomial around a depth of 20,000 (9,507-30,301) |

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}
# dependencies = TRUE also installs vegan and ggplot2, used below
BiocManager::install("repdist", dependencies = TRUE)
```

```{r libs}
library(repdist)
library(vegan)
library(ggplot2)
data(simulate_cog, package = "repdist")
```

# Inputs

A real analysis starts from three files, which `simulate_cog` holds as
objects; each step below gives the file-based code commented out above the
code that runs here. Only the first call, `embed_proteins()`, needs the
model, so it does not run in this vignette.

## Proteins and their embeddings

A FASTA file of the proteins identified in the samples: one record per
protein, with the protein ID as the first word of the header (`>WP_1.1
description` gives the ID `WP_1.1`). `embed_proteins()` reads it and returns
an `AAStringSet` with one embedding per protein in
`mcols(proteins)$embedding`. Its first call downloads the model (up to a few
GB), and the 110 proteins here take about 40 seconds afterwards on a laptop
with an Apple M-series GPU. `known_models()` lists the models, and
`read_fasta()` reads and checks a FASTA file.

```{r embed}
# not run: downloads the model on first use
# proteins <- embed_proteins("path/to/proteins.fasta") # model = "tmvec"
# the same, for this vignette's FASTA:
# proteins <- embed_proteins(system.file("extdata", "simulate_cog.fasta",
#     package = "repdist"))
proteins <- simulate_cog$proteins # embeddings precomputed
proteins
dim(S4Vectors::mcols(proteins)$embedding) # proteins x embedding dimensions
```

## Counts

A table of counts, such as spectral counts or PSMs, with one row per sample,
one column per protein, sample IDs in the first column of the file and protein
IDs as the column names. Every protein in the table needs an embedding with
the same name; proteins in `proteins` that no sample holds are ignored.

```{r counts}
# counts <- as.matrix(read.delim("path/to/counts.tsv", row.names = 1,
#     check.names = FALSE))
counts <- simulate_cog$counts
counts[1:3, 1:3] # samples x proteins
```

## Sample table

One row per sample, in the row order of the count table, with the design
variables to test.

```{r samples}
# samples <- read.delim("path/to/samples.tsv")
samples <- simulate_cog$samples
head(samples, 3)
```

## Annotation

`simulate_cog$annotation` has one row per protein and is not an input of
`repdist`: it holds the answer, so that the results can be scored. Its
columns are `protein` (the ID), `role` (`GrpE` for the ten treatment proteins
or `background`), `enriched_in` (the sample a GrpE protein is spiked into),
the COG assignment (`cog`, `cog_name`, `gene`, `category`), `length`,
`organism`, and `mmseqs30`, the protein's MMseqs2 30%-identity cluster.

```{r annotation}
annotation <- simulate_cog$annotation
head(annotation[, c("protein", "role", "enriched_in", "cog", "gene")], 3)
table(annotation$role)
```

# Protein bins

Bins group structurally similar proteins and use only `proteins`, so this
section stands alone: it needs no count table. `protein_similarity()` builds
the graph that `bin_proteins()` clusters. It takes every pair of proteins
whose embeddings have a positive cosine similarity and aligns the two
sequences. A pair becomes an edge, weighted by its predicted TM-score, only
if its alignment E-value is at most 0.01, the number of equally good
alignments expected by chance when searching all of `proteins`. The
embedding says the proteins may share a structure and the alignment says the
similarity is not an accident of the model, so an edge needs both.
`bin_proteins()` splits that graph by Markov clustering (MCL) and returns each
protein's bin (`membership`), the proteins of each bin (`clusters`) and each
bin's medoid (`representatives`). Bins are named `bin1`, `bin2`, ... from
largest to smallest, and a protein with no edge is a bin of its own.

```{r bins}
# aligns every pair with a positive similarity: quadratic in proteins
S <- protein_similarity(proteins, progress = FALSE)
bins <- bin_proteins(S)
table(size = lengths(bins$clusters))
```

Most bins are single proteins, as they should be: the 100 background
proteins come from unrelated COGs. The GrpE labels were not used to build the
bins, so they can score them: coherence is the share of the GrpE proteins in
the bin that holds most of them, and purity the share of that bin's proteins
that are GrpE.

```{r scores}
grpe <- annotation$protein[annotation$role == "GrpE"]
grpe_bin <- names(which.max(table(bins$membership[grpe])))
c(coherence = mean(bins$membership[grpe] == grpe_bin),
    purity = mean(bins$clusters[[grpe_bin]] %in% grpe))
```

All ten GrpE proteins fall in one bin, although they share no more than 30%
sequence identity pairwise (34 of the 45 pairs still pass the alignment
gate). `plot_bin_similarity()` shows the weight of every pair inside a bin;
a grey cell is a pair that is not an edge.

```{r bin-plot}
#| fig.width: 6
#| fig.height: 5
#| fig.alt: "Predicted TM-scores between the proteins of the GrpE bin"
plot_bin_similarity(bins, grpe_bin, S)
```

# Beta diversity

Beta diversity compares samples. Three distances follow, each on relative
abundances: MMD on the embeddings (`sample_mmd()`), Bray-Curtis on the
proteins, and Bray-Curtis on the bins. MMD needs only `counts` and
`proteins`; the bins are used only for the third.

## Relative abundances

Dividing each sample's counts by its total removes the difference in
sequencing depth between samples. It does not remove its effect on which
proteins were seen.

```{r relative}
relative <- counts / rowSums(counts)
```

## Sample-to-sample distances

`sample_mmd()` represents each sample as its relative abundances over the
protein embeddings and returns the distance between those distributions as a
`dist` object. `vegdist()` gives Bray-Curtis between samples; `bin_glom()`
sums the proteins of each bin first, for the bin-level version.

```{r distances}
D <- list(MMD = sample_mmd(relative, proteins),
    `Bray-Curtis (protein)` = vegdist(relative, "bray"),
    `Bray-Curtis (bins)` = vegdist(bin_glom(relative, bins), "bray"))
```

## PERMANOVA

PERMANOVA (`adonis2()`) tests whether the group centroids differ, with 999
permutations. R² is the share of the distance variation that the grouping
explains.

```{r permanova}
permanova <- lapply(D, function(d) {
    set.seed(1)
    adonis2(d ~ group, data = samples)
})
knitr::kable(data.frame(R2 = vapply(permanova, function(a) a$R2[1], 1),
    p = vapply(permanova, function(a) a$`Pr(>F)`[1], 1)), digits = 3)
```

Protein-level Bray-Curtis does not detect the enrichment: it compares
accessions, and each GrpE protein is in one sample only, so to it the
enrichment is noise. Both structure-aware distances detect it. MMD credits
the ten GrpE proteins for being close in the embedding space and needs only
the embeddings. Bray-Curtis on bins counts them as one feature, and needs
the alignments of `protein_similarity()` first.

## PERMDISP

PERMANOVA responds to a difference in spread as well as in centre, so
PERMDISP (`betadisper()`) tests the spread on its own.

```{r permdisp}
permdisp <- vapply(D, function(d) {
    set.seed(1)
    permutest(betadisper(d, samples$group))$tab[1, "Pr(>F)"]
}, numeric(1))
round(permdisp, 3)
```

Group A is more spread out under MMD and protein-level Bray-Curtis, as the
design builds in: each group-A sample carries a different GrpE protein, and
no group-B sample carries one. On bins the GrpE proteins are one feature, so
the spread is the same in both groups. Where PERMDISP is significant, the
PERMANOVA is partly a test of spread, so read R² with the plot below.

## Principal coordinates

Principal coordinates (`cmdscale()`) place the samples in two dimensions so
that their distances are kept as well as possible; each group's outermost
samples are joined by a line (its convex hull).

```{r pcoa}
#| fig.width: 9
#| fig.height: 3.4
#| fig.alt: "PCoA of the samples under MMD, Bray-Curtis on proteins and Bray-Curtis on bins, group convex hulls"
pcoa <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(D), function(k) {
    data.frame(samples, cmdscale(D[[k]], k = 2), distance = k)
}))
pcoa$distance <- factor(pcoa$distance, names(D))
hull <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(pcoa, ~ distance + group), function(d) {
    d[chull(d$X1, d$X2), ]
}))
ggplot(pcoa, aes(X1, X2, colour = group)) +
    geom_point(size = 2) +
    geom_polygon(data = hull, fill = NA) +
    facet_wrap(~distance, scales = "free") +
    labs(x = "PCo1", y = "PCo2") +
    theme_bw()
```

The groups overlap under every distance: the enrichment is 5% of the
abundance of ten of the 110 proteins, and R² is 0.15 under MMD, so the test
finds a difference that the plot only hints at.

## Plotting without the most abundant regions

`plot_pcoa()` draws the same MMD ordination for a real dataset, where a few
very abundant proteins, such as elongation factor Tu, can dominate the
distances. It leaves out the `drop` most abundant regions before the PCoA. A
region is a group of proteins linked by predicted TM-scores of at least
`min_sim` (0.9), so that near-copies of one protein count as one; a message
names the most abundant protein of each region and its size. The choice
ignores the group labels and is for display only: test on the full distance
above.

```{r plot-pcoa}
#| message: true
#| fig.width: 5
#| fig.height: 3.4
#| fig.alt: "PCoA under MMD without the two most abundant protein regions"
plot_pcoa(counts, proteins, samples$group, drop = 2)
```

Here the two most abundant regions are single background proteins, 18% of
the abundance, and dropping them gives a cleaner separation than the full
distance does. `drop = 0` draws the full distance.

# Differential abundance

`bin_glom()` sums the counts within each bin. Any differential abundance
method can take the bin table; here a linear model per bin on the centred
log-ratio (CLR) of the counts, with a pseudo count of 1, and
Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment (q). LFC is the log2 fold change of group A
over group B. Bins with p < 0.05:

```{r da}
bin_counts <- bin_glom(counts, bins) # samples x bins
da <- function(m) {
    clr <- log2(m + 1)
    clr <- clr - rowMeans(clr)
    group <- factor(samples$group, c("B", "A"))
    fit <- t(apply(clr, 2, function(y) {
        summary(lm(y ~ group))$coefficients["groupA", c("Estimate", "Pr(>|t|)")]
    }))
    data.frame(feature = colnames(m), LFC = fit[, 1], p = fit[, 2],
        q = p.adjust(fit[, 2], "BH"))
}
res <- da(bin_counts)
knitr::kable(transform(res[res$p < 0.05, ], LFC = round(LFC, 2),
    p = formatC(p, format = "g", digits = 2),
    q = formatC(q, format = "g", digits = 2)),
    row.names = FALSE)
```

The GrpE bin, `r grpe_bin`, is the only one that survives the adjustment
(q < 0.05); the other bins with p < 0.05 are what chance gives among
`r nrow(res)` tests. The same model on single proteins finds nothing, since
each GrpE protein is abundant in one sample only:

```{r da-protein}
per_protein <- da(counts)
c(proteins_q_below_0.05 = sum(per_protein$q < 0.05),
    smallest_GrpE_q = min(per_protein$q[per_protein$feature %in% grpe]))
```

# Choosing parameters and cost

- **`max_evalue`** (default 0.01) is the edge gate of `protein_similarity()`.
    It is relative to the total length of `proteins`, so one value is stricter
    on a larger set. On this data 1e-5 gives 98 bins, with 9 of the 10 GrpE
    proteins in one; 0.01 gives 94, with all 10; and 10 gives 25 bins. It
    matters more for sets with many distant relatives.
- **`inflation`** (default 2) of `bin_proteins()` sets how fine the bins are,
    higher values giving finer ones. Here 1.4 gives purity 0.77 and 2 or 4
    give 0.91; a bin's purity is what annotation, if you have any, can check.
- **`sigma`** of `sample_mmd()` is the kernel bandwidth. The default is the
    median distance between the proteins (1.14 here, wider than any
    TM-score), and the value used is returned as `attr(, "sigma")`. For
    TM-Vec, `sigma = sqrt(1 - t)` puts the kernel's `1/e` point at predicted
    TM-score `t`: `sqrt(1 - 0.9)` makes only near-identical folds similar and
    here lowers R² from 0.15 to 0.08.
- **Cost.** `protein_similarity()` aligns every pair with a positive
    similarity and `sample_mmd()` holds a protein-by-protein kernel, so on
    real data use the proteins identified in your samples, never a whole
    search database. At 20,000 proteins the kernel alone is 3 GB and
    `sample_mmd()` needs at least twice that at its peak; the alignments,
    scaled from 40 minutes for 5,000 proteins on 10 cores, take about 11
    hours on 10 cores (`n_cores`).

A bin is not guaranteed to hold one function. The GrpE bin also holds a DnaK
protein, GrpE's HSP-70 partner, joined to it by a single edge with a
predicted TM-score of 0.31, which the alignment gate let through;
`plot_bin_similarity()` shows such an edge.
